title: How much can a distance-only gap say
subtitle: G2 lecture 141000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: The free-beam model separates low and high spectral clusters by an ordered gap.
body: That configuration supports sharp constant-one Sylvester estimates. What changes when two spectra have a positive pairwise distance but interlace rather than lie on opposite sides of one gap? This is the question Davis and Kahan raise in Question ten point one. It asks how sharply we can control the angle of a trial subspace using a residual if we know only that every trial spectral value is at least delta away from every complementary exact spectral value. The Sylvester equation illustrates two distinct difficulties.

slides.title: The compressed equation returns
slides.lead: Let E map the trial coordinate space isometrically into our Hilbert space.
body: Let F one map the exact complementary spectral space into that Hilbert space. The trial compression is A zero, and the exact complementary compression is Lambda one. Form the residual by applying the original operator to E and subtracting E times A zero. Project that residual onto the exact complementary space. Because that space reduces the exact operator, the projected residual equals Lambda one times F one star E, minus F one star E times A zero. Call X the map F one star E and C the projected residual. We obtain the Sylvester equation Lambda one X minus X A zero equals C.

slides.title: Pairwise separation solves the scalar equations
body: Choose orthonormal eigenbases of Lambda one and A zero. Write their eigenvalues as lambda i and alpha j. In those coordinates, the Sylvester equation says that lambda i minus alpha j, multiplied by the entry X i j, equals C i j. If the two spectra have pairwise distance at least delta, then every denominator has absolute value at least delta. Thus each entry of X has absolute value at most the corresponding entry of C divided by delta. That immediately proves a Frobenius estimate: square all entries, add, and take the square root. Delta times the Frobenius norm of X is no greater than the Frobenius norm of C.

slides.title: Why operator norm is harder
slides.lead: Now attempt the same proof for operator norm.
body: The inequality on each matrix entry is still true, but operator norm is not the maximum absolute entry. It depends on how entries cooperate when the matrix acts on a vector. Entrywise multiplication by a bounded coefficient matrix is called a Schur multiplier. Its operator norm can exceed the largest absolute coefficient. That is exactly what happens when the inverse Sylvester operator divides entries by different signed spectral differences. We can demonstrate the failure in two dimensions without approximation. Take A to be the diagonal matrix with entries one and minus one. Take B to be the diagonal matrix with entries zero and two.

slides.title: Ordered separation changes the proof
slides.lead: Suppose instead every eigenvalue of Lambda one lies at least delta above every eigenvalue of A zero.
body: Then we can use a single exponential integral. The solution X is the integral, from zero to infinity, of the semigroup generated by negative Lambda one on the left and positive A zero on the right, acting on C. In other words, every component decays with its spectral difference. The entire operator integrand is bounded by the norm of C times exponential decay at rate delta. Integrate that scalar bound and obtain one over delta. This proof works for operator norm and compatible ideal norms because we estimate the whole product of operators, not its entries separately.

slides.title: What survives without order
slides.lead: For self-adjoint spectra that are disjoint with a positive distance, the inverse Sylvester operator can instead be represented using oscillatory unitary groups and a Fourier kernel.
body: The scalar kernel reproduces the reciprocal of a frequency away from the forbidden gap around zero. The reciprocal Fourier kernel has an integrable absolute value that yields an operator-norm estimate with the constant pi divided by twice the gap under the stated separated self-adjoint spectral hypotheses. The proof is more delicate than entrywise division.

slides.title: Read Question ten point one precisely
slides.lead: The historical question asks how sharp a residual-to-angle theorem can be under distance-only spectral separation.
body: Theorem six point two gives constant-one Hilbert-Schmidt control under its spectral separation assumptions. The broader operator-norm story requires different techniques and constants. Our two-by-two example rules out a universal constant-one result in operator norm. We must also specify which angle we control. X equals the exact complementary projection composed with the trial inclusion. It records directed sines.

body: Theorem six point two gives constant-one Hilbert-Schmidt control under its spectral separation assumptions. The broader operator-norm story requires different techniques and constants.

slides.title: What to retain
slides.lead: Any claimed improvement must identify its three-block hypotheses and the norm in which the interacting overlaps are measured.
